speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: PENSIONS AND SOLDIERS' PROBLEMS
speechtext:
The question of the appointment of counsel representing the Canadian branch of the British Empire Legion is one matter; the appointment of counsel to represent returned soldiers is another. I think I intimated that such counsel should be appointed, but he should not be under the instructions of the legion. He should be there

maintopic: EXCISE ACT AMENDMENT

speechtext:
Hon. W. D. EULER (Minister of National Revenue) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution :
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Excise Act to provide for power to examine witnesses on oath, and to pay their reasonable travelling expenses; for the imposition of duty on screened malt computed on the quantity after it has been removed from the kiln and screened; for making certain offences indictable, and such other amendments as are deemed necessary for a more adequate enforcement of the act.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: EXCISE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I think the hon. gentleman
might make a statement with regard to this resolution.

maintopic: EXCISE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the provisions of the bill are not many; they are designed almost entirely to clear up some problems and some inconsistencies which have developed during the administration of the act. There are one or two additions all of which, as I say, are designed to make the working of the act more clear with regard to certain weaknesses which have developed. I think possibly if hon. members would allow the motion to pass, the information in detail can be given much better a little later on. I can assure hon. members that the additions which are being made are very simple in their nature and do not involve any great principle at all.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Johnston in the chair.

maintopic: EXCISE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I suppose this resolution
has received the approval of His Excellency the Governor General?

maintopic: EXCISE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Yes, the matter has been
brought to the attention of His Excellency the Governor General and his consent has been obtained.

maintopic: EXCISE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: If we adopt this resolution we agree to the principle of all that is contained in it, and it covers rather a wide range. Would the minister be good enough to take the points one by one and let us know just what are the explanations, in order that we may follow them in their relation to the present act? For instance there is the question of examining witnesses on oath. I understood that the act covered that already. What is the need for that amendment, and wherein does it amend the present act?

maintopic: EXCISE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
That particular provision
arises almost directly out of an investigation which was held in Halifax last year, to which reference was made at the close of the session by the leader of the opposition. We found then that our own officers had not power to examine witnesses under oath, and an order in council was necessary to give them that power. In outlying sections of the country it will make it very much easier if the officers have that power. I do not see how anyone
Excise Act Amendment

can possibly be prejudiced in the matter, and certainly it will make the work of the officials of the department a great deal easier.
The next amendment, providing for the payment of reasonable travelling expenses, explains itself pretty well. The proposition to impose duty on screened malt is to do away with the present condition whereby coomings and screenings are compensated for by a refund after the goods have been imported. We are going to do away with that altogether, so that no duty will be paid on the screenings but only on the net result after the screenings have been removed. Then there will be no necessity for refunds. I am not sure that I can add anything more.

maintopic: EXCISE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: What offences are to be made indictable?

maintopic: EXCISE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: This arises out of a situation which came up in connection with a certain tobacco company which was caught selling cigarettes without the payment of excise tax. They were fined and promised to amend their ways, but they did not do so. It was discovered that they had recommenced the practice and under the circumstances it was thought advisable to seize their stock, but a considerable doubt arose as to whether we could do so legally. I think the house will agree that in offences of that kind it should be possible for the department to deal more summarily with the offenders than has been the case in the past. We are practically without a remedy; people even move goods out of customs bond without any adequate punishment.

maintopic: EXCISE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: What other amendments are deemed necessary for the more adequate enforcement of the act? That is rather a sweeping power that the minister is requesting.

maintopic: EXCISE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: If I wanted to give my hon. friend full information I would have to give him a resume of the bill itself. The bill is very short; I do not know whether or not my hon. friend has it before him, and I hardly suppose the committee would wish me to recite the provisions which are contained in the bill itself.

maintopic: EXCISE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: This is not captious criticism at all; the point is that the minister undoubtedly has a rather extensive bill which will follow this resolution. We do not want the minister to come back at us later on, when we query him on the bill, and say, " Well, you agreed to this in the resolution."

maintopic: EXCISE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I will give my hon. friend the assurance that I will not find fault with anything he may wish to ask later on.

maintopic: EXCISE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: This is a very sweeping sort of blanket cheque we are giving; the minister simply asks for such other amendments as are deemed necessary for the more adequate enforcement of the act. We have not the faintest idea of what that is intended to cover. So as far as I am concerned I want the minister to understand that in agreeing to the resolution, when the bill comes up it does not mean that we will not give it the fullest examination.

maintopic: EXCISE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
We will not have any disagreement on that.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Euler thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 48, to amend the Excise Act.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS

speechtext:
Hon. PETER HEENAN (Minister of Labour) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to bring in a measure respecting fair wages and hours for labour employed by contract or otherwise on public works of the Dominion of Canada.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Johnston in the chair.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext: The bill which is proposed to be introduced contains three distinct features. It will establish current rates of wages, provided that in all cases they must be fair and reasonable, which is a new feature in our fair wage policy. It also provides that the eight hour day shall apply to contractors, and it also takes in government employees on similar work, as provided for by the bill. When the bill is before the committee we will be able to give any details required.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think these matters should be considered before the bill is presented to the house. I have received a telegram from an important firm of builders and contractors who state that there are clauses in the bill which would be a possible source of serious embarrassment. These contractors suggest that the construction industry

Fair Wages and Hours
be permitted to submit their views before a bill is presented to the house. I hope the minister will consider receiving suggestions from employers of labour in reference to the clauses of this bill.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext: Will the hon. member state the name of the firm who forwarded that communication ?

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext:
I have not received permission to divulge the name, but neither has any objection been offered, so I presume it would be quite in order for me to state that the name of the firm is John Flood & Sons, Limited, of St. John, N.B. Perhaps it would be better to read the telegram. It starts off by calling me "Honourable." Under ordinary circumstances I would not have mentioned that, but evidently they are taking a keen interest in the progress of events. The telegram reads as follows:
Learn Hon. P. Heenan moved resolution respecting fair wages and hours labour on public works contracts.
That would appear to be previous information as the resolution was moved to-day.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext: They are an up to date firm.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext:
The telegram continues:
Have memo of bill draft and note provisions which are objectionable to construction industry and possible sources of serious embarrassment.
I would direct the attention of the minister to the following:
Suggest construction industry permitted submission views before bill drafted.
In view of the position which these people occupy in the community, and in view of their discernment with regard to the member to whom they sent the telegram, I would urge again favourable consideration by the minister.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it will be quite proper for any citizen of Canada to make representations regarding this measure, but I do not see how those representations can be made until the bill is printed. A representative of that firm of contractors has interviewed me regarding the bill and I told him that he would be at liberty to bring any delegation at any time after the introduction of the bill. I think the hon. member will realize that no one can discuss the bill until it is introduced and printed, and I can assure my hon. friend that after that time we will receive any delegations in connection with this matter.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext:
They do not ask to present their views on the bill, they ask an oppor-

tunity to present their case before the bill is drafted. The minister should have the opinion of those who are interested before he drafts his bill as it is easier to make changes at that time.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the minister if this bill will be referred to the standing committee on industrial relations, or is it proposed to deal with it in the committee of the whole?

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext:
I think it would be only
fair to those who are interested in this bill that they be given an opportunity to be heard. If the minister does not agree with the position taken by the hon. member for St. John-Albert (Mr. MacLaren), then I would suggest that this bill be referred to a committee of the house.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext:
I would rather introduce
this bill as a government measure and take the responsibility than meet the wishes of representatives from all over the country. This is a government measure and it will be dealt with in the committee of the whole.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext:
The government seems to
have one policy for one class of bill and another policy for other bills. This is a bill which will vitally affect business in this country. If it were a political plaything which the minister had in mind, I could well understand that he would not-

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext: Order, order.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext:
There is nothing wrong
about that. That seems to be exactly what he has presented-a political baby is now to be born. If the minister intends to pursue the line of conduct he has indicated, I would suggest, in the interests of business and in the interests of the men themselves who labour on public works, that the whole thing should be referred to the committee on industrial relations where the views pro and con can be discussed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext:
We ought to see the
baby before sending it away like that.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext:
We can well apprehend
the character of anything that comes from the Minister of Labour.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext:
A few days ago in committee of supply, hon. members from the maritime provinces complained that fair wages were not being paid on certain government con-
Fair Wages and Hours

tracts being carried out there. Now we have an hon. member from the maritimes (Mr. Hanson) complaining of the action taken by the government.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext: I cannot allow that remark to pass. I was not the gentleman who took that stand, in fact it was the hon. member for Inverness (Mr. Macdougall) and I am sorry that he is not here to-day to speak for himself. I have not expressed any opinion as to the merits of this measure, and the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) has no right to ascribe wrong motives. In fairness to all concerned, not only to the contractors but to the men themselves, as well as to the taxpayers of this country who, after all have to pay the bill, this bill should be referred to a committee of the house where views thereon could be presented.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the department is eleven years too late in bringing forward this measure. Eleven years ago the city of Toronto adopted an eight hour day and the union or prevailing rate of wages, on contracts which is 60 cents per hour. Nothing is done regarding aid to unemployment until we have an election pending, and then the government decides that something must be done to appeal to the labouring class. This bill is brought down eleven years after the large municipalities in the province of Ontario had adopted not only a fair wage clause but the eight hour day in all civil contracts. The minister in regard to that particular amendment has no way of enforcing it. How is he going to enforce this proposal? What penalty will be placed in a contract to enforce it? Many contracts to-day are dead letters. A great deal of this work is being sublet; a contractor gets a job and sublets it to someone else. As I said last night, the Alien Labour Act is a dead letter in this country. Contractors are bringing into Ontario unskilled labour from all over Europe, and the government and the fair wage officer seem to be asleep because they are nowhere to be found nor can they enforce the contract.
No credit is due to the government for bringing in this legislation. It has been forced upon them by what was done by the provinces and the municipalities in 1919 and 1920. The city of Toronto provides for an eight-hour day and in every contract is inserted a fair wage clause, providing for the union or prevailing rate of wages, which in Toronto is sixty cents an hour for unskilled labour.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext: After the bill is introduced, will there be an opportunity on the second reading to suggest extensions or amendments to it? I am not objecting to the bill; I am supporting it, but I do not want to be confined to the resolution and not be able to suggest amendments.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext:
I notice my hon. friend
(Mr. Adshead) says that he has no objection to the bill as it stands. I did not know the .bill was distributed. I would like to have had the same opportunity of seeing it and I would perhaps be able to discuss the matter more intelligently. The minister may tell us in a moment just to whom the bill has been distributed and who has had an opportunity of seeing and examining it. It would be interesting to know that.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext: The bill has not been in the possession of anyone but members of the government. It has not been distributed.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext:
A memorandum of the
draft bill has been handed out. Messrs. John Flood & Sons say that they have seen it.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext:
All I can say is that if
they have, I do not understand it, because the bill has not been distributed from our department.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext:
In the first place, I do not think there has been any occasion for this bill. The government, all through its history, should have been practising the principle enunciated in the resolution. I have in my hand a letter from The Building Trades Council, Vancouver. It is addressed to me and it reads:
We have been instructed to draw to your attention an anomaly in the methods adopted by the Dominion government in carrying on the construction of public works, viz: when calling for tenders from the various contractors the fail- wage clause is a component part of the contract, therefore it becomes compulsory upon the contractor to pay the established or current wage of the district in which he is doing government work; and in the event of any dispute regarding wages the government fair wage officer is empowered to enforce the act. However, on the other hand when the government undertakes to carry out its own construction work by day labour a different procedure is initiated and the fair wage clause is not given the slightest consideration. The men so engaged are hired in most cases at a considerably lower rate of wages than a contractor would be compelled to pay for the same class of work.
This is manifestly unfair because it debars members of the various mechanics' unions from accepting employment on government work when such work is being carried out by day labour and the matter does not end here, as the standard of living which has been built up by organized labour in this Dominion is

Fair Wages and Hours
imperilled. We would therefore respectfully request that you bring this anomalous condition to the attention of the government and have the act so amended that it will definitely rule; that the fair wage shall be paid on all government work whether undertaken by contract or day labour.
The point I wish to bring to the attention of the minister is this; he gives us no adequate information in the resolution as to the contents of the bill. In reply to questions he has stated: "Well, when the bill comes in, you will see it." He prefers to put the bill in as a government measure and force it through the house. This is a case where there is a definite and reasonable complaint that in certain instances where contractors do government work a fair wage clause is included in the contract. The fair wage clause calls for conditions prevailing and wages paid in the various branches of work in the community in which the contract is awarded, but on government work done by day labour, according to this letter-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext:
Does he cite the cases he has in mind?
Mr. STEVENS; I have read the letter.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext: That is a very general statement.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext: It is the generality of it that is somewhat alarming.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext:
If a man
wrote a letter of that kind I would expect him to set forth some specific case.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext: I do not agree with the minister nor with the "Hear, hear." This is an old dodge.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext: It is not.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext: It is-to say, when a member brings something to the attention of the house, name the specific case; name the particular job.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext: There is never a letter read on this side of the house but that complaint is made by hon. gentlemen opposite. I think it is a perfectly fair and proper question. If my hon. friend's letter makes an assertion, it should give the particulars.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext:
I have not the particulars and I am now making a statement based on the letter. The statement I am making is this: I think it is an exceedingly unwise and unfair policy for the government to carry out work under conditions that are different from those that are imposed upon a contractor
working on government work, should the work be let by contract. I have other letters on this subject; I have looked for them in my desk, but I find I do not have them under my hand. Does the minister cover that point in the bill which he proposes to base on the resolution which is very brief and incomplete? It says simply that it is-
A measure respecting fair wages and hours for labour employed by contract or otherwise on public works of the Dominion of Canada.
That is a very broad, sweeping statement. It might be a revision up or a revision down. You cannot get any information from it. Will the minister say whether the particular point I have mentioned has been covered in the resolution?

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext: Evidently the hon. member was not in his seat when I made my first explanation, or perhaps I did not make myself understood, because that is one point I explained. This will apply not only to contractors or employees engaged by contractors but also to employees of the government on government work.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext: Will it apply to government employees in the Public Works department?

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext: For instance, on dredging machines and so on?

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext: Is it to be provided that they get a fair wage and also holidays?

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext: Perhaps I had better explain. It is to provide that every contract with the government of Canada for construction, remodelling, repair or demolition of any work shall be subject to the fair wage conditions. Those are the contracts, and any employees of the Dominion government itself engaged on similar work will come under this bill.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext: May I ask if the fair wage proposed is a minimum wage or simply the going wage in the district?

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext: The current wage, the minister says.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext: It applies to current wages that are paid in the district, with this added provision, that in all cases the wages must be fair and reasonable. That is new.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext:
That does not mean anything. I have a specific instance that just came to my notice to-day. I should like to read a paragraph from a letter that I received
Fair Wages and Hours

from Canon F. G. Scott of Quebec, with regard to conditions in Grand-Mere. He speaks of the generally bad conditions there owing to the large number of people being out of work through the closing down of the paper mill, and goes on to say:
The government is building a new post office. At present only the foundation work, outside work, blasting, etc. is being done. I am told on good authority that the workmen are being paid at only 20 cents an hour. . . . Probably a contractor has got the job. Could you bring it before the house? The poor people are desperate and forced to work for anything.
In a district like that, where there is a lot of unemployment, and where wages apparently have been definitely forced down, it would seem as if the going wage is not an adequate safeguard. I think if we are going to have anything of this kind at all, we ought to have a definite minimum wage based on the cost of living.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext: Is this bill being introduced in substitution for the draft bill submitted by the trades and labour congress?

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext: The trades and labour congress did present a draft bill to the government. The bill based on this resolution does not include everything that the trades and labour congress had in mind, but it does take in most of the important features of their draft bill, and a good deal of what is left out is covered by other acts and regulations, such as the water powers regulations, section 244 of the Railway Act, and our own regulations of the Labour department.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext: In answer to a question the other day, the minister told me that the bill submitted by the trades and labour congress had been declared by the Justice department to be ultra vires. Are any such sections included in this bill?

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext:
I think that the questions, submitted by the hon. member for St. John-Albert (Mr. MacLaren) and by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) should in some way be answered, because one of the large firms of contractors upon public buildings here in Ottawa, who are also contractors on the Welland canal, have alleged that their financial position, they being presently in the hands of receivers, was brought about by the arbitrary action of a minister of labour who changed the terms of their wage contracts with their employees, and thereby brought about their financial destruction. That is their contention. Whether 
it is right or not, I cannot say. It did occur to me, however, listening to the minister, that he is dealing with a matter that has received the approval of almost every member of parliament. If I turned to Hansard, I should find that practically every member who has spoken on the subject has urged that it was not only desirable but essential that the government should have the same hours of labour and pay the same wages on its works as other contractors. That is based really on the obligation of the treaty of Versailles. That, I think, is unquestionable. The important question to answer, it seems to me, is what effect this bill may have upon existing contracts, where contractors have employed sub-contractors on certain terms as to wages? This resolution does not touch that at all, which I think is an important question to be answered, because as I have already said, one large firm of contractors claims that its present financial position is due to a minister of labour changing the rate of wages to be paid to their employees.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext:
The agreements now in
existence contain specific provisions, and this bill will apply only to future contracts.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext: Quite so. That is what I would suppose.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext:
About ten minutes ago
I asked the Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) a question, and I have not received a reply. I stated that I wholeheartedly supported the bill so far as it went, but that it did not go far enough. Will there be an opportunity on the second reading to offer amendments to the bill?

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS
speechtext:
Every member of the
house will have a right to offer amendments when we are in committee.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Heenan thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 49, respecting fair wages and an eight hour day for labour employed on public works of the Dominion of Canada.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE

speechtext:
The house resumed from Monday, March 31, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mackenzie King for committee of supply, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Heaps.

Unemployment-Mr. Church

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The amendment of the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) to the motion for committee of supply, reads as follows:
That in the opinion of this house the government should take immediate action to deal with the question of unemployment.
If we wait till the government takes action, we will wait till doomsday, because they have had all the opportunity they want to take action on this matter, and are incapable of doing anything to give relief or adopting any constructive policy.
Last night I was pointing out to the house what had been done in the United States, under the Hoover administration, to deal with the question of unemployment in a constructive manner. I showed that unemployment came under three heads-cyclical, seasonal and technological. By technological unemployment is meant the unemployment caused by the application of new machinery to industry, thereby displacing man power. Professor E. A. Stewart, of the State Agriculture College, university of Minnesota, says:
Machine-farming developments from 1850 to 1920 have released approximately 27,000,000 workers l'rom agriculture. Picture the undeveloped state of our cities, industries, transportation, and above all the entire absence of our modern sanitary and labour-freeing homes if we were still required to produce our agricultural crops as we did one hundred years ago. It takes but little imagination to picture our now beautiful cities, as a peasant country, ground down under long hours of toil, poorly educated people, faced periodically with famine and pestilence, with simple labour-killing homes for our families to live in. if farming were now carried on as it was in 1830.
While our population in 1950 may be six times as great as in 1850, yet it is conceivable and probable that the decrease in the number of farm workers which started to take place in 1910 will continue, and by 1950 no more farm workers will be required to supply food for a population of 150,000.000 than were required in 1850 for a population of 25,000,000.
This shows the inroads that machinery is making on manual labour. Now, the Minister of Labour says to our municipalities: "We have not anything to do with unemployment; go and see the provincial authorities." Then in turn the provincial authorities tell the municipalities, "Go and' deal with unemployment yourselves." If the Dominion government is not concerned with unemployment, what is the necessity of a Department of Labour? Surely its function is to protect the working classes, to secure jobs for them, instead of neglecting their interests and forcing them to go in their hundreds of thousands to look for jobs in a foreign land. The federal government through its immigration department spends a vast amount of money 2419-73
in advertising in England and in bringing in immigrants, and then these people are left to shift for themselves. Unemployment means that most of our factories are running only half time while others are closed down altogether. No doubt Canada is a wonderful country, but what are we going to do about this unemployment? It is no good to tell starving men about the great natural resources of the country ; they want work to maintain themselves and their families. The unemployed call for bread, and get a stone and no work.
As I said last night, the United States are dealing with this problem of unemployment in a large, constructive way. They are conducting an active warfare not only on seasonal unemployment but on this newer form, known as technological unemployment, brought about mainly by the introduction of machines that supplant the worker. But what is this government doing to solve the problem? They should be in a state of active warfare all the year round against unemployment. In time of war we mobilize all our resources to overcome the common enemy at the gate. Now, in time of peace, let us mobilize all our resources against the economic invader; let us preserve our home market for our own working men. Is the government doing this? No, the pan-American tariff of the government is throwing our workers out on the street. In short, the government say, "We have nothing to do with unemployment; that is a matter for the provinces." No doubt they rely on section 92 of the British North America Act which declares that the establishment, maintenance and management of hospitals, asylums, charities and eleemosynary institutions are in the jurisdiction of the provinces.
There are several causes for the very serious condition of unemployment that we are now passing through. One is the pan-American tariff that I have already referred to. We have been told that Liberalism is the open road. Of course it is. Liberalism is the open road to the LTnited States for many of our workmen as well as for many of our technical and professional men. Last year the Prime Minister told us that in relation to United States tariff matters we must keep a cool head. Now, after a year of this cool-head attitude what is the fiscal policy of the government to-day? It is a cold-feet policy towards the aggression of the United States. Mussolini has said that Italy will pay back the Ignited States in her own medicine; France will do the same. This country? Well, we are suffering from the cool-head-cold-feet tariff policy of the government. We may as well take a leaf out

Unemployment-Mr. Church

of the book of Mr. Hoover, for all is fair in the race for business. Let us tell the people of the United States that we can no longer continue the one-sided "reciprocity" relationship with that country that we have tolerated for the past twenty-five years. The United States have conducted an economic warfare against this country for the last fifty years, making Canada the dumping ground for their manufactured products in exchange for our raw products and' man power; and this man power is of much more importance to the future of this country.
Another cause of the present unemployment is lack of technical education. This government says it has nothing to do with technical education. Then there is the lack of any proper policy of scientific and industrial research. Scientific research does not consist in building a great monument of stone and having a research council with a lot of figureheads-mostly doctors. I have been trying to find out what kind of a doctor Doctor Skelton is; he is in the exterior department. Then we have Doctor Tory, who is a Tory in name only, in the research department. Our policy is all wrong. Let us adopt the policy of the British government in this regard. Instead of frittering away millions of dollars on buildings, let us devote the money to medical science, bio-chemistry and other lines of research by grants to the universities.
The government seem to have a lot of specialists in the immigration department. Well, if they were only as successful in immigration as they have been in emigration I should have no fault to find. The former head of that department has been rewarded with a seat in the other chamber. The only cure the government has provided for unemployunent is the "ambassador" cure. We have ambassadors in Washington, Tokyo and Paris, with their first secretaries, their second secretaries, their third secretaries, while thousands of our college graduates have had to go to the United States. The government's tariff policy seems to be that nothing that can be bought in the United States should be manufactured in Canada, especially in eastern Canada; and that everything that cannot be bought from the United States should be imported from Europe especially from Germany. That policy has helped to fill the ranks of the unemployed. There is no unemployment in Germany to-day, nor in France or Italy. Why? Because each of those countries has adopted a constructive fiscal policy. The government have no coal policy. Instead of fifty or sixty million dollars going to the American coal barons it should go into the pockets of the coal miners of Alberta and

Wales and the maritime provinces. We have a national railway7. What are they doing for unemployment? Their policy of immigration has brought thousands of Europeans into this country.
In the Canadian Pacific Railway system we find Canadians in office, from the top down, but in our government owned system we have many Americans. In the first place, there is Mr. Gaston, a young lawyer from Yale, who is brought in to take the office of vice-president of the Central Vermont line. As a matter of fact, Gaston seems to be a very popular name with the government of this country.
The Minister of Finance claims that he is a low tariff man; the same applies to the Minister of Railways. The Minister of Railways and the Minister of Finance seem to be in a low tariff way the Alphonse and Gaston of the prairies. The policy of the government has been that anything that can be bought in the United States must not be bought in Canada, and especially, in eastern Canada. According to this policy if it cannot be bought from the United States, it should be bought from Europe. Is it any wonder that with such conditions we have unemployment in this country?
One of the unfortunate features of unemployment in Canada is that the workers are forced to lower their standard of living. Another feature is that the state of unemployment has the effect of lowering the morale and self respect of the workmen. Unemployment is a problem of industrial organization, and it is not a problem confined to the operations of individuals; it is a persistent factor in modern life. The industries in Canada however, that can give regular employment to their workmen, even in times of prosperity, are few indeed. From a report I have in my hand I find that from one million to six million people are out of work in the United States, one million is the minimum and once it was six million.
When President Hoover was faced with an unemployment situation he called the heads of industries together in order to arrive at a satisfactory solution of the problem, but we find no such constructive policy adopted by the government of Canada. Instead of the Minister of Labour trying to stem the tide of unemployment, and summoning industrial leaders, he does nothing. As a matter of fact, the government was asked in this house a few days ago if it would hold a conference to relieve the present situation, and it refused.
Unemployment in Canada is the price society is paying for progress, and in many instances it may be traced to efficient management. Many are out of work to-day in

Unemployment-Mr. Woodsworth
this country because of the progress of modem industry, and revolutionary changes in Canada. Unemployment is caused by methods of manufacture which make it no longer necessary to produce goods by manual labour. Out of this condition we find decay in society which formerly was prevented because of the need of labour. The efficient executive finds that by eliminating the service of a certain class of labour he improves and increases his output.
A considerable amount of unemployment occurs at more or less regular intervals. Such a situation is due to business depression, and to seasonal ups and downs. Such unemployment is constant. Men are thrown out of work regularly, and because of this the subject needs constructive treatment. They lose their work because of financial failures which are occurring and the removal of plants from one end of Canada to the other. This situation requires attention. Where is the Minister of Labour? What is he doing, when this situation exists in our country. We have hundreds of thousands of bushels of wheat in the western elevators, stored up for distribution on the world market. But what is the situation? We find when the price of wheat goes down, the price of bread remains stationary. What is the Department of Public Works doing towards relieving the unemployment situation? What is being done on the national highways, or on the St. Lawrence waterway?
The Canadian Pacific Railway is doing its part to help unemployment and has voted the sum of $50,000,000 to aid the unemployed and for reconstruction. The Canadian National Railways does not take this as an example, however. Thomas Bradshaw, the president of the Massey Harris Company has returned from Europe, and he advocates a marketing board for Canada; but the government will have nothing to do with it. If we were across the border the president of the United States would not take five minutes to find a cure for the problem which faces us. In Canada, however, we do nothing; we refuse to cooperate with industrial leaders. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, the government should set up a commission for this purpose.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, year after year, we in this comer, have tried to bring the question of unemployment to the attention of the house.
I think we have to admit that this year the volume of unemployment is greater than it has been for some years. It seems to me most unfortunate that our statistics show the amount of employment, but give very little 2419-73A
indication as to the amount of unemployment. The statistics simply show the number who on a given date are employed, but does not show the number left out. To my mind this is an important item of statistics, and we should have from the Department of Labour the actual statistics as they apply to this subject. There is little doubt, however, that the situation is serious at the present time. A few weeks ago we had a delegation which waited upon the government, composed of officials of nearly all the cities in western Canada; a week or two later there was a similar delegation from the city of Toronto. I need not go into the figures which they presented to the government, as they have been published already in the press. Undoubtedly we have a large amount of unemployment today. Last fall I was through twenty or thirty cities and towns of Ontario, and I found that even some of those places which hitherto had been comparatively free of unemployment were complaining of it at that time.
We may as well face the fact; we have unemployment. I will say very frankly that I would not blame the government for this condition of affairs; unemployment exists not because of administrative defects but rather because of great economic forces over which no government has very much control. The government may and does claim credit for prosperity; I think they take altogether too much credit for prosperity when it exists. I do not much wonder that people who have been taught to praise the government for prosperity will hold the government accountable for hard times when they come, and I think possibly the government will find that out to their sorrow before many months go by. However, as I say, I do not blame the government for this condition; I think we would have a very large measure of unemployment at the present time no matter what government might be in power. Unemployment is not limited to Canada; we have it in the United States to a very large degree, and our conditions are more or less similar to those which exist in that country. We have it in Great Britain as we all know, and we have it in almost every country in Europe. It is a world phenomenon.
Further I should like .to say that I think we should get beyond the stage where we say the unemployed are to blame for the condition in which they find themselves. Many are unemployed through no fault of their own. Again and again we hear people getting impatient with the unemployed and regarding them as the next thing to criminals. I quite admit that there are a certain number who
1148	COMMONS
Unemployment-Mr. Woodsworth
are lazy and shiftless, but I would say that laziness is itself one of the outstanding results of unemployment. A man who is out of work or who gets only an occasional job for weeks and weeks is not going to continue to be a very good worker, but the fact is that the great majority of the men who are unemployed to-day were employed when work was available, and they would be employed again if work were forthcoming.
Anyone who has been engaged in social work cannot help but be impressed by the hopelessness of the condition in which the ordinary worker finds himself when out of a job. I have been more or less closely associated with the unemployed of my own city for the past twenty-five years. Sometimes we have had more and sometimes less unemployment, but every year in the winter time we have people who are praying that the spring may come in order that they may earn enough to buy something to eat for themselves and their families. Some years ago I was engaged in institutional work, where little children in the kindergarten were being fed at noon because they had insufficient nourishment at home, and some of them were unable to keep on their stomachs the cocoa that was given them, because having been accustomed to only the poorest kind of food the milk cocoa was too rich for them. I say it is no less than a disgrace in this country that year after year we allow maladjustments of this kind to continue. I have stood in a line with the unemployed, and from the scores whose stories I have learned personally, I know that many of these people are only too glad to get a job if the job offers. I remember one day when a few jobs were being passed out to a crowd of one or two hundred men. One man standing beside me was passed over; he gulped and the tears came to his eyes, and as he turned away he said, "I would not mind so much if it were not for the kids." I sometimes wonder, as we sit here in our comfortable chairs and listen to statistics and talk about great policies, whether we recognize quite clearly enough what this unemployment really means in the terms of human worry and human suffering.
We have to-day men in the building trades employed for only six, seven or at most eight months in the year. What are they to do during the other months? They are absolutely helpless in my part of the world; there are no other jobs offering. When the factories close, as they are closed now in some parts of Ontario, what can the man with a little cottage and a family do? He cannot move out to some other part of Canada; he would
[Md. Woodsworth.]
be just as badly off if he did so. He has to remain where he is, and his family may suffer. Consider the coal miners in Alberta, from whom I am getting heartbreaking letters almost daily, asking that something be done. If these companies cannot market their coal what is the poor miner to do? He cannot move anywhere else; he has to stay there and suffer, and naturally he looks to some authority to do something for him.
Last fall in my own city and my own constituency, where the Canadian Pacific Railway has very large shops, within a few days nearly a thousand men were laid off. What could these men do? Their families were there, it was the beginning of winter, and they could not possibly move out. The situation became more and more desperate in the little village of Brooklands, which is a part of my constituency, on the outskirts of Winnipeg. The municipality began to help, but the municipality consisted of the people themselves and it was poor. One of the last things I did just before coming to Ottawa was to meet a deputation which came to see me, consisting of the mayor and councillors of this little village, who asked that if it were at all possible something should be done for them in the way of relief. Already most of these men have mortgaged themselves to the limit, and they wall have to work all this summer to begin to pay their grocery bills.
In this country we must recognize the fact that a considerable amount of unemployment is seasonal in character. Whether or not we admit it to the outside world, in western Canada at least we have a cold climate, and many kinds of work slacken up or cease altogether when winter comes on. Farm labourers are turned off after the harvest, and these men have nothing else to do. Bush work does not open up until later, and at all events there is not so much bush work offering as there was work for harvesters, so these men drift into the cities and increase the problem with which the cities are already struggling.
But I would say that deeper than any of these things I have mentioned is the fact that the unemployment situation seems to be inherent under the existing capitalistic system. We forget that this system, through which the greater part of the productive machinery is concentrated in the hands of a few, is a comparatively new system in the history of the world. In the old days each individual worked with a few tools, produced for himself and consumed pretty much what he produced, or exchanged his products with his neighbours. I am not going into the history of all that was involved in the industrial revolution, but

Unemployment-Mr. Woodsworth
we all realize that we have an absolutely different state of affairs now from that which existed one hundred or two hundred years ago. Our present system is comparatively new, and we have not yet adjusted many things in it so that they meet the needs of the mass of the people.
Take for example one phase of this situation, the wonderful productivity of the machine to-day. Roger Babson, the well-known statistician, in a recent article in the Cambridge Tribune, stated that since 1914 such progress has been made that to-day thirty men can produce as many motor cars as one hundred men could produce fourteen years ago; forty men can produce as many rubber tires as one hundred men could produce fourteen years ago; in the iron and steel industry forty men can produce what one hundred men produced fourteen years ago; and in metals other than iron and steel sixty men can produce as much as one hundred men could produce fourteen years ago. In varying degrees this is the experience in industry generally. Along this line, I could quote some interesting statistics from the January, 1929, issue of Manufacturing Industries, a copy of which I hold in my hand, but I do not intend to take up the time of the house in doing so. We all recognize how the machine has changed the entire situation, but perhaps most of us have not realized the effect of that change in our own agricultural areas. Let me quote some statistics which a friend of mine procured for me in Saskatchewan, as follows:
On the farms in Saskatchewan, according to the 1926 census, there were 26,674 farm tractors; m 1927, 5,727 tractors were sold; in 1928, 8.703. making a total of 41.104 farm tractors, which means roughly that practically one-third of the farms in Saskatchewan employ tractors. Not only do these tractors apparently displace a number of men but their operation requires men with some mechanical ability and some experience in the operation of tractors, which is evident by the fact that tractor companies conduct schools throughout the province during the winter in the handling and operation of tractors.
In addition to the tractor there is the growing tendency for placing machinery on the farms, as a result of the development of the internal combustion engine and availability of electrical energy. A newer development of farm mechanization is the introduction of the combine. In 1926 there were 148 combines operating in Saskatchewan; in 1927 there were 382; in 1928, 2.679 and the estimate of the Implement Dealers Association for 1929 places the number of combines for this province at between 3,500 and 4.000. Each of these machines will, at a conservative estimate, displace four to six men. They reduce the harvest operation on an ordinary farm, for cutting, stooking and threshing, from a period of possibly ten to fifteen days to five or six days. The total number of these combines in 1928, in the three western provinces was 4,716.
A few years ago immigration was advocated for the west as a means of supplying farm labour, but to a considerable extent that labour is not needed to-day, and in many cases the men brought in are not fitted to do the work which is now required. I wish I had time to give to the house an outline of those books which have become almost standard, such as Tawney's The Acquisitive Society, and Sidney Webb's, now Lord Passfield, The Decay of Capitalist Civilization. I wish hon. members would remember that such social maladies, if I could call them that, as unemployment are part of this system under which we are now living. Some of us are enjoying great privileges under this system; perhaps the whole race is enjoying a higher standard of living, but large numbers of people are suffering because of these maladjustments.
I wish I had time to speak of the larger proportion of production which is going back to fixed capital. A few years ago I mentioned the book of Mr. J. A. Hobson, entitled Economics of Unemployment. He takes the position that although at first our present system may have enabled us to accomplish a great deal more by concentrating wealth in the hands of the few, as this process has gone on and has been extended, not merely to Europe but to almost all parts of the world, we have the phenomenon of a great deal more being produced than the people can purchase, of a very large amount being put back into fixed capital so that the fixed capital is out of all proportion to the commodities produced. That is an economic argument which I think might be considered.
I do not see why we in Canada should not have established a permanent economic commission to carry on research in this particular field. Failing that, it seems to me that we might very well appoint some sort of a joinm parliamentary committee, which might sit even between sessions, as I think is done in some parliaments. This committee would be composed of representatives from various parties in the house and would be able to give definite study to questions of this kind. ,
I do not intend to dwell upon the financial aspects of unemployment, but I would like to quote a paragraph to show what some people think of the underlying financial reforms that might be made. I read from an article entitled Banking Credit and Unemployment as
1150	COMMONS
Unemployment-Mr. Woodsworth
published in the International Labour Review of January, 1924, as follows:
There is a growing school of economists whose attention is mainly directed toward the possibility of stabilizing industrial activity by judicious regulation of the bank credits upon which industry is largely dependent.
And again:
Bank credit, the main agency through which the community may add to its purchasing capacity, might be regulated, not, as previously, in accordance with mechanical and virtually uncontrollable processes, but in accordance with the broadest interests of society as expressed by a scientific combination of indexes of trade and employment.
When one mentions anything of this kind he is apt to be regarded by the house as more or less of a faddist or crank, and yet these views are being put forward by a large and growing school or series of schools of economists. The subject has been thought worthy of study by the League of Nations.
Unemployment in other countries is brought about by their own local conditions, but our difficulties have been aggravated by our immigration policy. Year after year I have tried to impress upon the house the serious condition which exists in the city of Winnipeg. I should like to read a clause or two from a resolution passed last autumn by the city council of Winnipeg, as follows:
Investigations disclose that a large number of those likely to be unemployed during the ensuing winter are immigrants who have been brought into the country within the past two or three years, and also some who have been put out of employment by the newly arrived immigrants for whom there was not sufficient employment without displacing those who were employed at the time of their arrival.
The responsibility is placed clearly, and these figures are borne out by the conditions obtaining in other cities of the west. Another resolution was passed by the city council which I think is rather interesting. Some hon. members may say that it is very socialistic in character, but it was passed by the Winnipeg city council. It reads:
That council petition the Dominion government- to take steps to shorten the length of the working day in order that available work be more widely distributed.

What is the date of that
resolution?

speechtext: It is signed by the mayor and by the city clerk and was passed early this winter. It is a petition to the governor in council of the Dominion of Canada by the mayor and council on behalf of the citizens of Winnipeg and1 of the province of Manitoba. I am sorry I have not the exact date.

speechtext: Did you say to lengthen or to shorten the working day?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That council petition the Dominion government to take steps to shorten the length of the working day in order that available work be more widely distributed.
We have been told again and again that unemployment is primarily a municipal or provincial responsibility. I quite admit that sixty years ago when a man was out of a job in a little rural area in Ontario or Quebec, this was clearly a local responsibility. I quite admit that in those earlier days when the great part of the population was resident in the country districts or in little villages and dependent upon the country for work, such a matter as unemployment was local in character and naturally would be attended to by the municipalities, helped out in an emergency by the province.
But the situation is entirely changed to-day, and when the Dominion government throws out of equilibrium our population by introducing hundreds of thousands, yes millions of people into this country, the responsibility ceases to be merely local in character and becomes Dominion-wide. Further, as long as the Dominion government so largely controls the country's fiscal policies which may make or unmake an industry, the Dominion government cannot avoid responsibility for ensuing unemployment. It is only in recent years that the present administration has undertaken to refuse all responsibility for social needs of this nature. After the Versailles treaty we find that the report on this subject of the draft conventions was submitted to the Governor General in council on November 2, 1920, by the Minister of Justice and that it was duly concurred in by the council and approved by His Excellency the Governor General on November 6, 1920, as follows:
Recommendation Concerning Unemployed
As to Number 3, the minister observes that the experience of other countries has demonstrated that a system of unemployment insurance, in order to be effective and successful, must be made ancillary or complementary to a system of labour exchanges, the whole being adapted to the principal function of finding work for unemployed insured workmen. In this view,-
And I would like to call special attention to this sentence:
-unemployment insurance has a pronounced federal aspect and on the whole the minister thinks the establishment of a system of unemployment insurance is competent to the Dominion in the exercise of its residuary legislative power with regard to the peace, order and good government of Canada.

Unemployment-Mr. Woodsworth
I for one am getting a little bit tired of being told by the government that almost any proposal is ultra vires. We are informed in case after case that this has been the declaration of some mysterious people-I do not know just who they are-called the law officers of the crown. When we have in 1920 the Department of the Minister of Justice making an important ruling of this kind, it ought not to be lightly set aside. If the British North America Act was drawn up sixty years ago, surely it ought to be the same in its interpretation for at least ten years and not to be dependent upon what one must more or less characterize as political considerations.
In speaking as I do to-day I am representing the view's not merely of the Labour group with which I am associated, but of a very large number of citizens of western Canada. I should like to read a paragraph from an editorial from the Manitoba Free Press of January 14, 1930. The Free Press on the whole, I think, has been favourable to the present administration. It says:
Senator Forke did not say anything very useful when he told the United Farmers of Manitoba that immigration was not responsible for unemployment. Technically he is probably right, but more than technicalities are needed to ward off unemployment. Most people will agree with Mr. A. R. MacNamara, Assistant Deputy Minister of Public Works for Manitoba, when he stated that so long as immigration is a federal affair, one of the keys to the unemployment situation lies in federal hands. He is undoubtedly right.
More than this, it is common knowledge that persons have come to this country on assisted passages with a "guarantee" of employment in their hands, and have found on arrival that hard times have made it impossible for the propeetive employer to give them jobs. What about these new arrivals? Are they a federal responsibility or are they not? There can only be one answer.
As for the Hon. Peter Heenan's contribution to the problem, the less said about it the better. Even if it is true that the provinces in conference in 1927 definitely stated that unemployment relief was a provincial affair, it does not make Mr. Heenan's position as Minister of Labour much better. The fact is that it is not a purely provincial affair. If the provinces say it is. it is up to Mr. Heenan to disabuse them on that point.
I think that is all I need to quote from the Free Press. I heartily subscribe to that view and instead of the Minister of Labour doing as he did a few months ago when he was asked to call a conference on unemployment, trying to sweep away the suggestion, he should have been in the very forefront endeavouring to champion the cause of labour and the unemployed. I would say to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), who has not yet said a word in this debate: He
may represent a constituency in western Canada, but he does not understand the spirit of the west if he thinks he can hide behind the British North America Act when such important questions as this are at stake.
Reference has been made by previous speakers to what the Minister of Labour said at London. I would be glad if by his speech he has given the public generally the idea that unemployment insurance in this country is needed. I suppose that would be a gain.
I know the impression has gone out that the Dominion government is about to bring in some measure of that kind. A friend of mine in Toronto, who is not a labour man but, as a matter of fact, a financial man, wrote to me a day or two after that speech saying: "I am glad indeed to find out that the Dominion government is taking action along this line.
I have written a letter to the Prime Minister to congratulate him on his action." He said- and he was speaking as a financial man-"I have always taken the ground that labour should have its reserve just as capital needs its reserve." There are many people outside the ranks of labour who are coming around to that point of view.
But whilst there may have been an advantage in the Minister of Labour setting a sort of ideal before the people of this country, it is little less than cruel to raise the hopes of the people unless in some way the government is prepared to back up the statement of the Minister of Labour. The Prime Minister is very fond of dilating upon responsible government, its great advantages and how it was attained. If we believe in responsible government and that the cabinet ought to be responsible for what is said by a minister, then the Minister of Labour ought to be held responsible for an important pronouncement such as the one he made at London. He ought not to give to the general public such a statement as that without being prepared to back it up, or if the report is not correct he should officially deny it. I want to read two or three paragraphs from the report of the Canadian Press. This particular item I took from the Toronto Globe, but a similar statement was in nearly all the papers east and west. This report is taken from the Toronto Globe of March 15, 1930, and reads:
Ottawa to Back Project for Unemployment Fund Heenan States at London
The Dominion government is ready to assist the provinces in establishing unemployment insurance for Canada on a contributory basis announced Hon. Peter Heenan, Minister of Labour, in an address here to-night. In making this announcement, Mr. Heenan said:
"As far as I am concerned, I will utilize my every effort, and the Premier will back me

Unemployment-Mr. Woodsworth
up, to see that the labouring man who is out of work for any period of the year will have a right to expect and to receive a share of the profits he helped make."
Mr. Heenan said that the nature of certain Canadian industries made it inevitable seemingly that there should be seasonal unemployment in certain occupations. The workers who are unemployed for perhaps two or three months of the year constitute an essential unit in the industrial life of the nation for the remaining periods, and the country should recognize their rights, he said. Mr. Heenan amplified his proposal to say that he believed that the worker, the employer, and the governments, provincial and federal, should each bear a part of the cost of such unemployment insurance.
Now I would like to ask, did the Minister of Labour say that? That is reported by the Canadian Press, and from coast to coast, the government was given credit for it. Did the minister make that statement? I hope that he did. If he did, did the Prime Minister state that he would back him up in that policy? I should like to have an answer from the Prime Minister himself before this debate goes very much further.

speechtext:
I think the Prime Minister ought to state his position, as well as the Minister of Labour. Further than that, there is a definite pronouncement that the Dominion government is prepared to give a certain amount to assist the provincial governments. Just to be accurate, let me read it again:
Mr. Heenan amplified his proposal to say that he believed that the worker, the employer, and the governments, provincial and federal, should each bear a part of the cost of such unemployment insurance.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: That evidently would not be a vicious principle.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: No, I do not think that, and I should like the Prime Minister to expatiate a little bit further on what he meant last year by vicious principle. I have read the Hansard only recently, and for the life of me I cannot see anything else than that after mature deliberation the Prime Minister believes that the granting of old age pensions was based on a vicious principle. I believe that he has subsequently denied that, or it is said that he has denied it. I should like him to state frankly what his position is in that regard.
