speechtext:
I shall be very glad to do so now. I thoroughly believe in old age pensions and in all that this government has done to support them. I would ask 
my hon. friend to produce any statement of mine on Hansard or anywhere else which will bear out his statement that I thought old age pensions were based upon a vicious principle.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I have not the page of Hansard.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: No, and you cannot get it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Will the Prime
Minister permit me to bring it before him later?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes, but you cannot find it anywhere.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I remember distinctly that there was an interruption by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner), and the Prime Minister replied. I referred to this last year.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: The interruption my hon. friend is referring to will not bear out what he is saying.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I shall be glad to get it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I do not know why my hon. friend should be so anxious to misrepresent me. He knows what my attitude is.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: The Prime Minister is hardly fair to me. I have not been unfair to him.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: You are unfair to me now.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I shall take the earliest opportunity possible of finding the page in Hansard and reading it, and I shall hope to do this early enough that the Prime Minister may be able to make his statement based on that Hansard record. I do not want to be unfair to the Prime Minister. What I thought was simply this: As the years have gone on, the Prime Minister has been so busy emphasizing the necessity of placing responsibilities on the provinces, that he has gradually come to the point where he feels that it would not be a good principle for the Dominion government to hand over grants to the provinces in the way that was done under the Old Age Pensions Act. If that is not the case, why I shall be delighted, because it may mean that the door will be open and that we may get other types of social insurance. I would say to the Prime Minister -he may think that I have no right to make the suggestion-that from the political standpoint he could not do anything better in this country than to grant some relief to the tens

Unemployment-Mr. Woodsworth
of thousands of people who are to-day having a very hard time through lack of employment.
I am not particular whether that relief comes from the Liberals or the Conservatives. We in our little corner are too small a group to hope to foe in a position for a great many years to come to bring in a money measure. We cannot do that, but we do urge one of the older parties that has the necessary numerical strength to do it. I should like to take advantage of this opportunity to ask the Prime Minister and the Minister of Labour to place very clearly before this house and the people of this country what their policy really is. I do not think it is fair that despatches of the kind I have read, should go out through the press to the people of this country from coast to coast, and then when we try to pin the speakers down to declare what they really mean to do, we get an evasive reply.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I made a frank reply to my hon. friend in the house, in answer to a question that he put to me. He knows that it is on Hansard. There is no evasion. It is as clear as day.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The Minister of Labour
says exactly the opposite of what the Prime Minister says.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: The Prime Minister's statement was clear, but it was not the same type of statement that he made the day before in the room where the deputation was being heard.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I beg my hon. friend's pardon. The statement was identically the same, and again I challenge my hon. friend to point to any authoritative source which will indicate that there is any difference. My hon. friend* is not fair. He is not following his usual custom; I will say that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I want to be fair.
I shall be glad to have this matter cleared up. I was present and heard the Prime Minister. We had no official Hansard there, but a great many people came out from the meeting under the impression that something would be done.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Something
very different from what my hon. friend is now saying.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Then the next day the Prime Minister refused, as he rightly said, to commit himself to definite action. But a few weeks later, the Minister of Labour goes out and says something very different from what the Prime Minister has said, and the Prime Minister so far has not repudiated what the Minister of Labour says.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: The Minister of Labour will make his own statement. My hon. friend was referring to me, and I was referring to what he said about me. He can find nothing on record anywhere to support what he says is my attitude with regard to old age pensions or unemployment insurance.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: The Prime Minister knows as well as any member of this house that on the theory of the collective responsibility of the cabinet, no responsible minister can make a general pronouncement of policy without committing the cabinet itself. The Prime Minister has not repudiated what the Minister of Labour has said.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: My hon. friend has not heard* the Minister of Labour yet.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I have read today the statement, in quotation marks, of the Minister of Labour that went out over the Canadian Press wires, and the Minister of Labour himself has not repudiated that statement. I want to get this situation cleared* up.
I should like the public to know whether the government does or does not intend to do anything along the line of unemployment insurance. If it does not, I think the people of this country will turn to somebody who will. On the other hand, if the government intends to go ahead with a scheme, some of us here are prepared to back them up to the limit. But we should like to know, and the public has a right to know, what the government proposes to do.
I do not want to go into the details of unemployment insurance. May I say simply that it is generally recognized the world* over that under the existing system, with the evils and maladjustments that have arisen, it has become essential that until some better system is brought in, some sort of unemployment insurance should be provided. Here let me give credit to the Prime Minister; he agrees with that position. Well then, I ask, what action may we expect the government to take at this time?

speakeroldname: Mr. J. T. THORSON (Winnipeg South Centre):
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I agree with a great deal-

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Let us have the Minister of Labour-Heenan.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: The member for Winnipeg South Centre has the floor.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Let us have
Heenan.	*

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I agree with a great deal of what has been said by my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth).

Unemployment-Mr. Thorson

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: It is time we heard from the government.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
With him I agree as to the necessity of a scheme of unemployment insurance. I believe in unemployment insurance, not as a panacea for unemployment, but as a means whereby the evils of it might be very considerably lessened. One of the most comprehensive editorials that has been written on this subject appeared in the columns of the Manitoba Free Press shortly after the unemployment conference that took place in Winnipeg in January of this year. May I quote one or two paragraphs from that editorial? It says:
The idea that unemployment can be entirely cured or prevented will not be entertained by anyone who recognizes the effect that economic changes and the invention of new machinery have had in the past, and will have in the future, in displacing labour, and who also remembers the weakness of human nature and the measure of incompetence and improvidence that it contains. The problem will always continue, and it is a question of reducing it as far as we can. In seriously attempting this, uo one will imagine that it can be accomplished by any single panacea. The problem must be attacked in many different ways and success will largely depend upon general cooperation.
I believe the statement that unemployment will always be with us is particularly true of a country subject to the climatic conditions that obtain in Canada. The editorial proceeds :
Although unemployment cannot be completely cured, the conscience of the present generation is impelling it to make the most intelligent and most resolute attempt to reduce the problem to much smaller limits.
In common with my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre, I agree that a system of unemployment insurance will have the effect of reducing the problem to very much smaller limits than those that exist at the present time. The editorial goes on:
The community hears the cry of the women and children and realizes the worry of men who are unable to help their suffering dependents It knows that unemployment begets poverty with all the unhappy social effects flowing from it. Apart from human compassion, there is the fact that the unemployment of labour is an economic loss and also that the conditions arising from unemployment result, directly or indirectly, in heavier demands upon our general hospitals, mental hospitals and jails.
Then the editorial goes on to consider where the responsibility rests:
What is the responsibilty of the Dominion, the provinces, and the municipalities? And in what way should they cooperate? The Dominion government cannot divest itself of a measure of permanent responsibility,-
[Mr. Thorson.1
With that statement I entirely agree.
-at least whenever unemployment becomes very acute in any section of the country. Apart from the duty of helping any part of the Dominion when there is real trouble there on a large scale, there are two counts on which the federal government has a responsibility for unemployment. It has control of immigration and the influx of more people than the country can absorb is sometimes the cause of unemployment. It is undoubtedly partly the cause of the present difficulty. Another ground for Dominion responsibility is that there are many ex-service men among the unemployed and some of them are there as a result of war service. If it were left entirely to the provinces and the municipalities to deal -with unemployment, and if one province did so more adequately than another, it would be inviting the unemployed to come to that province. With federal cooperation the provinces would all be better able to meet the situation and this trouble would not arise.
The Dominion then has a certain definite responsibility and should be ready to cooperate whenever unemployment becomes too great a burden for the municipalities and provinces. How can that cooperation be given? It can provide work by proceeding with public works and by having the government railway system make a special effort to proceed with improvements. And it can also contribute a percentage of the cost of unemployment relief that is undertaken locally. It may be a bad principle, as Premier King says, for the Dominion to make grants to the provinces and lose control of the spending of the money, but it is a practical expedient which is necessary to meet serious unemployment situations.
So much for Dominion responsibility. Then the editorial deals with the responsibility of the provinces and municipalities:
The provinces have a responsibility because there is always a certain drift of the unemployed within the province, particularly to the larger centres, and the burden cannot fairly be left to them to bear. And the unemployment of their own people is sometimes so great in some municipalities that they have a proper claim upon the province for assistance. The municipalities, of course, are brought directly face to face with the problem. They cannot evade it because it is pressing upon them and they must cope with it as best they can, and with all the cooperation they can obtain. But unemployment is often due to general rather than local causes, and it is unreasonable to leave too great a burden upon the municipalities.
What can the municipalities and the provinces do to lessen unemployment? They can encourage such developments as will ensure a large element of stability of employment. The fact that many of the unemployed in Winnipeg this winter have been farm workers shows that the encouragement of mixed farming, which would keep more farm workers employed all the year, is one practical way of stabilizing employment in Manitoba. The municipalities and the province can also deliberately plan to have as much work available in the winter as possible. Are there other ways in which the Dominion, the provinces or the municipalities can cope with the problem?

Unemployment-Mr. Thorson
Then the editorial deals with the responsibility of employers with regard to unemployment:
The railways, manufacturers, public service corporations, and other employers also have a very definite responsibility to maintain the greatest stability of employment possible and to avoid, wherever possible, the laying off pf workers for certain periods. They cannot, in this generation, treat their workers simply like equipment that can be used or laid aside when not required. They must have regard, and must feel a direct responsibility, for the welfare of their workers. A great deal has been accomplished when there was a real effort towards stability of employment, and great hardship and suffering have often resulted from the lack of such effort. The principle should be accepted of every industry or business endeavouring to carry all its permanent employees and making that a charge against the business.
The editdrial proceeds with a statement which I think is very important, and with which I entirely agree. It is this:
Finally unemployment insurance must be regarded as one inevitable means of dealing with seasonal unemployment in Canada. Under our constitution, apparently, it must be undertaken by the provinces. Should the constitution be amended to enable the Dominion to contribute, since the Dominion has a responsibility in the matter? With the workers, the employers and the government sharing the cost, the workers would be protected against the annual loss and hardship due to winter unemployment. It would be one of the most effective means of dealing with the situation.
I do not propose to analyze the causes of unemployment, or to lay down any rules that ought to be followed in any attempt towards a solution of the problem. I doubt whether the problem will ever be solved, in our present state of distribution of the proceeds of labour and of our national wealth. There are some things, however, which are not the causes of unemployment. The editorial goes on to say:
It is hardly necessary to say that unemployment in Canada or elsewhere is too serious a matter to be treated as a partisan political issue. The suggestion that the problem can be solved simply by raising the tariff and giving greater protection to Canadian producers is answered by referring to the situation in the United States, highly protected and yet with some 3,000,000 workers now unemployed; or to Australia, whose tariff has been raised from time to time for the specific purpose of offsetting unemployment but whose new government finds that unemployment is still very serious, and proposes to apply the old remedy although a recent royal commission expressed the opinion that, while the tariff had been beneficial to Australia, it had been raised too high and was hampering and injuring the country. There is no such cure for unemployment. It must be attacked in various other ways. It is an urgent human problem that demands the best thought that can be given it, and the most practical forms of cooperation that can be devised.
This house has placed itself on record on a number of occasions as being in favour of the principle of unemployment insurance. Reference has been made from time to time to the powers of the Dominion on the one hand, and of the provinces on the other, in regard to this matter. Much as my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre may deplore the fact, the British North America Act is of importance in connection with this subject. May I indicate wherein the difficulty lies?
I do not think there is any constitutional objection to the Dominion government participating in the cost of unemployment insurance, in so far as that cost ought to be borne by the state. The Dominion government now contributes to the cost of old age pensions, and it could with equal right contribute to the cost of unemployment insurance. There is a constitutional difficulty, however, that is fastened upon us by the British North America Act; we are subject to certain restrictions. I use the expression "fastened upon us" advisedly, because it frequently happens that our federal system is an absurd arrangement so far as national progress and development are concerned. I would not be in favour of any scheme of unemployment insurance which is not based upon compulsory contributions towards the cost of it by the employer on the one hand, the workman on the other, with the state as a third contributing party. There is no doubt whatsoever that it is beyond the constitutional powers of this parliament to enact a scheme of unemployment insurance which can effectively compel employers and workmen to contribute to the cost of such a scheme.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Would it not be
possible that the Dominion government could say that if such a scheme were set up it would be willing to make a contribution?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am coming to that
phase of the question. No scheme of contributory unemployment insurance can be validly effected, in so far as it is a general scheme, without the cooperation of the provinces in the project. Therefore, while there is undoubtedly a large measure of responsibility for unemployment resting upon the federal government, there is also the necessity of having the provinces enter into such a scheme, because no scheme of unemployment insurance is likely to be accepted by this country unless it is contributory in its character. We must admit that it is beyond the legislative powers of this parliament validly to enact such a contributory scheme.

Unemployment-Mr. Thorson

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: It would be a scheme which would be dependent upon concurrent contributions, in the manner the hon. member has mentioned.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes, and the cooperation of the provinces would be necessary.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Does not the hon. gentleman think it is the duty of the federal government to initiate that very thing?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I would be very strongly in favour of the Dominion government initiating such a scheme.
The situation I have described was realized by those who drew one of the resolutions that was presented to the unemployment conference held recently in Winnipeg. The resolution to which I refer was moved by Thomas E. Moore, an alderman of the city of Port William, and seconded by Thomas W. Malloy, who represented the government of Saskatchewan. The text of the resolution is as follows:
Whereas after an exhaustive enquiry by a committee of the federal government recommendation was made for the establishment of an unemployment insurance scheme for the whole Dominion; and
Whereas the law officers of the crown expressed the opinion that under the British North America Act the federal government cannot inaugurate such a scheme; and
Whereas there is urgent necessity for the establishment of an unemployment insurance scheme;
Therefore be it resolved that this conference endorses the principle of unemployment insurance, and urges the calling of an inter-provincial and federal conference at the earliest possible date for the consideration of the adoption of a Dominion-wide scheme.
There are various methods that might be adopted in setting up such a scheme. We might follow, for example, the course we took when we enacted the Old Age Pensions Act. We set up the machinery for the administration of the old age pension system, and then said, in effect, to each of the provinces, "You may come into this scheme; you may apply it to your province or not as you choose." We might follow a similar course with regard to inaugurating a system of unemployment insurance. One of the difficulties with regard to such a proposal was voiced at the unemployment conference in Winnipeg last January when Mr. MacNamara, assistant deputy minister of public works for Manitoba, said:
Infirmly believe that no city or province dare vorK out a comprehensive unemployment scheme without making that city or that province the Mecca for the unemployed beyond its boundaries. Any scheme must be undertaken in all parts simultaneously. It has been suggested that unemployment insurance is the cure. Fancy any one province undertaking a scheme like that on its own.
[Mr. Thorson.)
That is one of the difficulties of setting up a scheme similar to the one that we set up with regard to old age pensions. Much hesitation might be- shown by any one province in being the first to come into such a scheme.
The suggestion has been made, however, by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps), that we might in this parliament set up machinery of the sort which I have indicated, and provide that it should not come into operation until three or four or five of the provinces have indicated their willingness to enter into such a scheme. That course of procedure, I think, would meet the difficulty which Mr. MacNamara suggests and at the same time would bring about the necessary cooperation between the Dominion on the one hand and the provinces on the other. With that suggestion of the hon. member for North Winnipeg I quite agree. I would like very much indeed to see proper steps taken towards the calling of an interprovincial and federal conference with a view to instituting such a scheme of unemployment insurance as that which I have endeavoured to outline.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot agree with my hon. friend for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth)-
Mr. GARLAND (Bow River)): Nor with the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Thorson), who has just spoken.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Perhaps not, but my hon. friend does not know yet what I am going to say. I cannot agree with my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre when he says that the cause of unemployment is the introduction of improved machinery.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I did not put it in just that way. I suggested that the improved machinery did bring about immediately a certain amount of unemployment, that it was one of the contributory causes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
We will let it
go at that. The introduction of machinery has had this effect. It has made production cheaper and has made it possible for a smaller number of men to produce the same amount of wealth. When we say that the introduction of improved machinery and methods brings about unemployment, we place ourselves in the position which the workmen took two or three centuries ago when the loom and the spinning jenny were invented. They thought these machines were going to take away their employment; therefore they proceeded to destroy them.

Unemployment-Mr. Young (Weyburn)

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: And so they did for the time being.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: For the time being.. but in the long run the result was more employment, and it was possible for the world to sustain a larger population in a greater degree of comfort because of the existence of those machines.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Kindergarten stuff.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Perhaps so, but my hon. friend would not be any worse for a little kindergarten teaching. I cannot agree with my hon. friend, either, when he says that a shorter day will solve the problem.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Again that is hardly what I said. I read a resolution passed by the Winnipeg city council, urging upon the government a shorter working day.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Do you not approve of it?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes, I do, but I do not say that would solve the problem.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: But you approve of the suggestion. Well, in my opinion a shorter working day would mean less wealth created in the world, less wealth for the people to consume; less food; less clothing, less of all the things that go to make real wealth, and therefore you would only aggravate the condition.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Then why not work a fourteen-hour day?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
If it could be demonstrated that by working a fourteen-hour day we could produce more than in a ten-hour day, I think we would be better off to do so. However, what I want to deal with at the present time is the particular condition in Canada at the moment, rather than unemployment in general.
I think at least hon. gentlemen opposite will agree that there is more unemployment in Canada to-day than there has been for some years past. What is the reason for it? The primary reason is that we had very poor crops last year. Railway employees were laid off and have been out of employment all winter, because there has been no wheat to move. Not only were railway employees laid off for that reason, but factory workers are also out of employment from the same cause. Those farmers who had wheat to sell found that the price had gone so low that when they had paid their necessary out of pocket expenses nothing was left for themselves. The purchasing power of the farmer has disappeared; he is not buying. If you would restore employment in this country the first thing to do is to restore the purchasing power of the farmer.
It has been suggested-in fact all the suggestions have been-that we should adopt some form of unemployment insurance, the cost of which would be contributed to by the workers, by the employers and by the government. I have no objection to any form of unemployment insurance which is to be supported by the workers themselves and their employers, but when you ask the government to contribute to the cost of that insurance I object.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Why?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I will tell you why. The unemployment situation has been worse during the last six months than it was the previous six months. It got worse in the fall, when it was found there was a very small crop to move, and that that crop had brought the farmer very little purchasing power. These men who were laid off had been employed for the previous six months, and were paid for every day they worked. The farmer worked the whole year. He did not receive his wages every week or every month. When the end of the season came he found that he was getting nothing for his year's work, and when you ask the government to contribute to an unemployment scheme you are asking that farmer, that man who for a whole year has been unemployed so far as receiving wages is concerned, to contribute to the support of a man who has been paid wages for at least six months.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: If the farmer has nothing how could he contribute anything?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is a very clever remark. I say the purchasing power of the farmer has gone. The farmer who had some wheat found that when he paid the necessary out of pocket expenses, that is, his threshing charges, his taxes and such things, nothing was left. The government takes a toll on everything that farmer buys, and out of that revenue it is proposed to pay a part of the cost of this unemployment insurance. The government has taken that toll from him and will continue to take it every time he buys anything.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I should like to ask one question. Is my hon. friend opposed to the idea of the Workmen's Compensation Act, which is unemployment insurance when that unemployment is caused by disability?
1158	COMMONS
Unemployment-Mr. Young (Weyburn) .

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Not necessarily, but that is another question entirely.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I should like to ask a question, which I think my hon. friend will not say is another matter entirely. Is he in favour of the provincial government backing the possible losses of the farmers through the wheat pool guarantee and is that not a possible contribution by unemployed labour as well as by farmers?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That is another
question entirely. I say that it is a rank injustice, and I protest against asking a man who has worked for a whole year and who has received no return for that labour to contribute to the support of a man who has been out of work for only six months. I have seen a farmer sell his entire crop at the end of the season and after paying his out of pocket expenses take every dollar of what was left and give it in wages to his hired man. I have seen that hired man go into the city and within two months he was flat broke, and I protest against the farmer being taxed to contribute towards the support of a man like that for the rest of the winter.

The Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) sits mum, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) sits mum, and no effort is made, except the smiles of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) to answer the amendment put forward by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps).
The government is going to sit there and manoeuvre politically to see what it can do to wiggle out of the situation in which it finds itself. It would almost let the question be put rather than answer the arguments made by the hon. member who proposed the amendment. It would let the unemployed tighten their belts a little bit more before it would enunciate to the country a policy which might relieve the situation. This session has taken the cake as far as political manoeuvring is concerned. The government has "on more: than one occasion sat back in order to see if it were possible to get hold of something apart 
from the general administration of the affairs of the country upon which it could hang an election issue. We have one instance after another which demonstrates its efforts to get away from the maladministration of affairs and to centre the attention of the people upon some side issue. The Minister of Justice looks towards me, and I suppose he would like me to talk about something which would be of interest to him.
The Prime Minister has intimated in previous years that he would bring down some legislation on divorce. After sidestepping several efforts which were made to force him to keep his promise, he asks an hon. member from Winnipeg to introduce a resolution and then, when the vote comes on, he asks the hon. member who sits directly opposite me to vote first, so that the press gallery and the country would not have the idea the government was taking any particular position upon the question raised in the house, as that question had been raised by a private member. Ask the country about anything and everything except the record of your administration during the last few years. The government will sit there and receive the benefit of the discussion upon this unemployment question and will not make any answer to the resolution which is equivalent to a vote of want of confidence. The government is enabled to pick out what valuable suggestions have been made, and then I suppose some member of the government will make a reply Do you call that following the mother of parliaments? Do you call that solidarity of government, when your back-benchers are put up to state their opinions before an official reply is made? As I understand a solid government it is one which, when challenged, immediately states its position in order that the other hon. members may know what it is. I suppose the government will state its position at the end of this debate when it has heard the representations made from all sides of the house as to what is best to be done.

Unemployment-Mr. Harris
Coming to the question under review, there is no doubt that considerable unemployment exists. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) has said, unemployment has been worse during the last six months than it was for the previous six months. It has been worse during the last six months than it was on January 28, 1926, when the hon. Minister of Justice rose in his place and stated:
-but the government is willing in ease of serious emergency, when a grave situation exists, to cooperate with the provincial and local authorities, and to bear a share of relief work or other relief measures which have to be adopted to meet a serious situation of that character, and we shall ask parliament to give us authority to that effect.
The hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) will admit that the situation is worse to-day than it was in 1926. If this condition exists, why was not something done when deputations came from all parts of Canada and asked this government to participate in unemployment relief in order to relieve an emergency. Not only did the government know about this condition, but during the months of December of last year and January of this year the press of the country were bringing this to the attention of the government. Even that good friend of the government, the Ottawa Citizen, had something to say in December. They reported:
Never before in the history of the city has the Union Mission, the hostel for indigent men, been so crowded at this season of the year as it is to-day.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre gave us the situation in Winnipeg. Four thousand single men and some four hundred married men with their families are being fed by the province and the municipality at Edmonton. The government knew that such a condition existed during December and January, but what is their answer to this plea? Statistics, the index figure of unemployment for September, October, and so on. It is claimed that this is not a federal responsibility but is a matter for the provinces. I think it was the Prime Minister who said that it was first for the individual, then the municipality, then the province, then the government. In other words, the individual who may be in a hopeless and helpless position due to unemployment has to wait until his municipality is in that same position; the municipality in turn is forced to wait until the provincial government has reached that stage; then when they have all reached that state of chaos this government will rise to the occasion and offer assistance for the relief of the situation. Is that fair? We are all one people.

In my opinion, before the hopeless individual finds himself helpless, policies should be enunciated; not economic argument but economic action to relieve the conditions in this country is what the hopeless and helpless individual wants and it is what the members of the government are on the treasury benches for. They are there to give us economic action, to see that these men are not left in this condition. When they are left in this condition through the world situation, the collapse of the stock market and-I will not say wheat pool manipulations but wheat pool activities, then the Minister of Justice, according to his utterance of January, 1926, can come to the relief of the situation, and parliament,

Mr. Speaker, at nine o'clock on Friday evening I was discussing the second reading of the bill, and had reached that point in my remarks where I was directing attention to the fact that in a great many cases before the Senate committee, paid agents were used to gather

Divorce Court for Ontario
evidence. I think that very often agents are used whose evidence might be questioned in courts of law.
Another point I intended to bring out was that anybody from the provinces of Ontario or Quebec who wished to procure a divorce through this parliament had first of all to go to a local lawyer, and then obtain an agent in Ottawa. Such procedure makes it more costly to obtain a divorce through this house than through a court of law. Further, if a divorce bill is turned down this year, the same bill may be brought up next year. If sufficient lobbying is not done it may not be passed the next year, and the result is that it has to be considered again and again. Had such a case gone to a court of justice and the judge ruled against it, it is questionable whether the case would be reheard. The judges in the divorce courts will not endeavour in any way to encourage divorce, and will conduct their cases in such a manner that the litigants must be very sure of their ground before instituting proceedings.
The committee of parliament in charge of divorce can rule only as to the dissolution of the marriage, it cannot grant alimony; it cannot rule on the disposition of the children, and no doubt in connection with many cases that come before the committee family troubles have arisen. For instance, the man in the case has proceeded against his wife for a divorce; she knows he no longer cares for her, and she will not contest the application. In such cases the divorce is granted, and the wife, who may be a mother is left without assistance for her children and with no way of gaining redress except by instituting action in some other court. On the other hand, if divorce proceedings in a case of that kind were taken in a divorce court, the disposition of the children, the settlement of alimony and sustenance for the family might be ordered. Evidence would be taken in camera, and the publicity experienced here would be avoided; the rules of evidence would be maintained as they are in the higher courts; decisions of those courts would be followed, and only the best evidence given by proper witnesses would be admitted; the king's proctor would be watching for collusion and cross-examining the witnesses; the interests of the petitioner and respondents would be protected, and no evidence would be given without cross-examination. These several things we avoid by having a divorce court, instead of bringing divorce before a 2419-744
committee of parliament and through the House of Commons.
For those reasons, Mr. Speaker, I intend to vote for the bill, and I hope it will pass as soon as possible.
